\[
I(x) = J(x)\, t(x) + A\, \big(1 - t(x)\big),
\qquad
\tilde{t}(x) = 1 - \omega \min_{y \in \Omega(x)} \min_c \frac{I_c(y)}{A_c},
\qquad
J(x) = \frac{I(x) - A}{\max\big(t(x), t_0\big)} + A,
\qquad
\omega = 0.95,\ t_0 = 0.1
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(I\): The hazy image, values from 0 to 1
- \(J\): The scene radiance, the haze-free image
- \(A\): The air light, one color for the whole image
- \(t\): The transmission, from 0 (all haze) to 1 (no haze)
- \(\Omega(x)\): The square patch around pixel x
- \(\omega\): The share of the haze that is removed
- \(t_0\): The lowest transmission used in the division

Haze mixes the scene radiance J with the air light A. The transmission t is the share of J that reaches the camera. It falls with distance. He, Sun and Tang observed that in most patches of a clear outdoor photo, at least one color channel is close to 0, in shadows, dark objects or saturated colors. That is the dark channel prior. So the dark channel of the hazy image, divided by A, measures 1 - t. The air light A is taken from the brightest 0.1 percent of the dark channel. It is the pixel there with the highest intensity, here the mean of red, green and blue. The raw transmission t tilde is blocky, since it comes from patches. The first paper refined it with soft matting. Its authors later showed that the guided filter does the same job much faster. Here the guide is the luma. omega keeps a little haze, and t0 keeps the division stable.
